📘 Guide: what each part means, why it is here, and when to use it

Click a topic to open it. The ⓘ button on each section jumps here. Educational only - these are ways to read the market, not buy/sell advice.

Daily routine - how to use this dashboard in 5 minutes

What it is: A simple order to read the dashboard, from the big picture down to single stocks.

Why it is in the dashboard: Each part answers one question. Reading them in order stops you from jumping into stocks before you know whether the market is supportive.

When to use it: Every trading day after 3:30 PM (or during the day in live mode), and before putting in new money.

How to read it: 1. Market regime: Easy, Balance or Hard Money? → decides how active to be. 2. Cards and signals: is breadth improving or weakening? Any divergence? 3. Breadth by group: are mid, small and micro caps joining? 4. Sector breadth and heatmaps: which sectors are strong or turning up? 5. Stock list: inside strong sectors, which stocks have high turnover, relative volume and are above their moving averages?   Big picture first, stocks last.

Time machine (date picker)

What it is: Moves the regime, cards, group table and sector table to any past trading day. Charts get a purple line on that date.

Why it is in the dashboard: Markets repeat patterns. Going back to important days (a top, a crash, a bottom) and seeing what breadth looked like then trains your eye to recognise the same setup when it appears again.

When to use it: When studying: go to a big market top or bottom and see what breadth, regime and sectors showed before and after. For a full past report with the stock list, use run_for_date.bat.

How to read it: Use ◀ ▶ to walk day by day and watch how numbers changed. Press Latest to come back.

Market regime - Easy / Balance / Hard Money

What it is: A one-word summary of market conditions. By breadth: Easy when at least 60% of stocks are above both their 10 and 20 DMA, Hard when 40% or fewer are. By index: Easy when the index is above its 10 and 20 SMA and at least 1% above the 20 SMA, Hard when below both and 1% or more below.

Why it is in the dashboard: Most stocks move with the market. The same setup works much better in an Easy market than in a Hard one. Breadth shows what most stocks are doing; the index can be pulled by a few heavyweights, so seeing both is useful.

When to use it: Check it first, every day, before any trade. Many traders take more and bigger positions in Easy Money, fewer and smaller in Balance, and mostly protect capital in Hard Money.

How to read it: Easy supportive · Balance choppy, be selective · Hard difficult, many setups fail. Index Easy but breadth Balance/Hard = narrow rally (few big stocks lifting the index) - be careful.

% of stocks above 10 / 20 / 50 / 200 DMA

What it is: Out of all stocks in the group, how many are trading above their moving average. 10 DMA = about 2 weeks, 20 = 1 month, 50 = 2.5 months, 200 = about 1 year. The card also shows the actual count, like '648 of 1,239 stocks'.

Why it is in the dashboard: It is the core breadth measure: it tells you whether the whole market is in an uptrend or only a few stocks. 10/20 react quickly (short-term swings), 50 shows the medium trend, 200 the long-term health.

When to use it: 10 & 20 DMA: for timing entries and exits (days to weeks). 50 & 200 DMA: for the bigger trend and deciding how much to be invested.

How to read it: ≥80% overbought - avoid chasing · 50-80% healthy · 20-50% weak · <20% oversold - bounce likely soon, wait for confirmation. Most useful: crossing back above 20% after a fall, crossing above 50%, and divergence (Nifty making new highs while these numbers make lower highs).

Advances / Declines and A/D ratio

What it is: Advances = stocks that closed up today, declines = stocks that closed down. A/D ratio = advances ÷ declines. The 10-day A/D ratio adds up the last 10 days to smooth out noise.

Why it is in the dashboard: Shows how broad today's move was. The index can be up while most stocks fall - A/D reveals that.

When to use it: Daily, especially on big index days: was the move supported by most stocks or not?

How to read it: Above 1 = more stocks up · below 1 = more stocks down. Above 2 or below 0.5 = a very one-sided day. A 10-day ratio staying above 1 = steady broad buying.

52-week new highs vs new lows

What it is: Number of stocks closing at their highest (or lowest) price of the past year.

Why it is in the dashboard: New highs show leadership and strength; new lows show damage under the surface. It often weakens before the index turns.

When to use it: When the index is near its highs (are new highs expanding or shrinking?) and after big falls (are new lows drying up?).

How to read it: Highs much more than lows = strong market. Nifty near a high but new lows rising = hidden weakness. New lows shrinking during a fall = selling pressure fading.

What breadth is saying (automatic signals)

What it is: Simple rules that check the numbers for you: regime changes, overbought/oversold, breadth thrusts, divergences, highs vs lows, and whether mid/small caps are leading or lagging Nifty.

Why it is in the dashboard: A checklist so you don't miss something important on a busy day.

When to use it: Read it daily after the regime. Treat it as a list of things to look at, not as buy/sell calls.

How to read it: green positive · yellow caution · red negative · blue information.

Breadth by group (All NSE, Nifty 500, Midcap, Smallcap, Microcap, BSE)

What it is: The same breadth numbers, calculated separately for each group of stocks. Nifty 500 = large + mid + small, Midcap 150, Smallcap 250 and Microcap 250 are the NSE size groups. All NSE = every NSE stock. In the NSE + BSE version: BSE only = stocks listed only on BSE, All India = NSE + BSE only.

Why it is in the dashboard: Smaller companies are the market's 'mood meter': they rise most when investors are confident and fall first when they get scared. Comparing groups shows how far participation has spread.

When to use it: Daily. Especially when Nifty is at highs (are small and micro caps confirming?) and after corrections (which group recovers first?).

How to read it: All groups strong = broad healthy market. Large caps strong but small/micro weak = risk appetite fading, rally narrowing. Small/micro turning up first after a fall = early sign of recovery.

Sector breadth table

What it is: Breadth for each NSE sector: % above DMAs, regime, change in % above 50 DMA over 20 days, advances/declines, 52-week highs/lows, sector turnover, turnover vs its 20-day average, and the average stock return (EW) over 1 week, 1 month and 3 months. Click a sector to see its stocks.

Why it is in the dashboard: Money rotates between sectors. Knowing which sectors are strong, weak or just starting to improve tells you where to look for stocks - and where to avoid.

When to use it: Daily or weekly, before searching for stocks. Also when the overall market is mixed: some sectors can still be in Easy Money.

How to read it: Strong sector = high % above 50 DMA and positive 20-day change. Turnover vs 20D above 1.5x = unusual money flowing in today. A weak sector whose 20-day change turns strongly positive = possible rotation starting. EW return = how the average stock in the sector performed, not just the biggest companies.

Stock list

What it is: Every stock with price, returns, volume, turnover and trend. Sorted by highest turnover today. Filter by sector (click a sector above), cap group, exchange, or conditions like 'Relative volume 2x'.

Why it is in the dashboard: After finding strong sectors, this is where you find the actual stocks - with the numbers that show where real money is moving.

When to use it: Daily, after checking regime and sectors. Use the filters to build quick watchlists.

How to read it: Click a name to open its TradingView chart. Use 'Columns' to switch between the volume/turnover view and the trend/moving-average view. The table shows the first 500 rows - use search, filters or sorting to find others.

Move vs normal and 55-day average move

What it is: 55D avg move = the average size of the stock's daily move over the previous 55 days (ups and downs both counted as size). Move vs normal = today's move ÷ that average.

Why it is in the dashboard: Every stock has its own normal movement - a large company may move 1% a day, a small cap 4%. The same 3% move is big for one and normal for the other. This makes moves comparable.

When to use it: Daily, to spot stocks doing something unusual today (news, results, breakouts, heavy selling).

How to read it: 1x = a normal day · 2x or more = unusual move (highlighted). Big move + high relative volume = strong conviction. Filters: 'Big up move' / 'Big down move'.

Volume and relative volume

What it is: Volume = shares traded today. Relative volume = today's volume ÷ the average of the previous 20 days.

Why it is in the dashboard: Raw volume can't be compared between stocks (Reliance trades crores of shares, a small stock a few thousand). Relative volume puts every stock on the same scale and shows when interest suddenly jumps - often when big players (funds, institutions) are active.

When to use it: Daily, together with price. In live mode remember today's volume is partial until 3:30 PM, so relative volume looks low early in the day.

How to read it: 1x = normal · 2x = double the usual (highlighted) · 0.5x = quiet. Price up + relative volume 2x+ = strong move with money behind it. Price up on low volume = weak, less trustworthy. Price down on high volume = heavy selling.

Delivery quantity, delivery % and relative delivery

What it is: In India, shares bought and sold on the same day (intraday) are not delivered. Delivery quantity = shares that stayed in someone's demat account at the end of the day. Delivery % = delivered shares ÷ total volume. Rel. delivery = today's delivery quantity ÷ average of the previous 20 days. Data comes from NSE's daily file (NSE stocks only).

Why it is in the dashboard: Volume alone can be mostly intraday churn. Delivery shows whether buyers are actually holding the shares - often longer-term investors or institutions accumulating.

When to use it: Daily, together with price, relative volume and turnover - especially on breakout days. NSE publishes each day's file in the evening, so in live mode today's delivery columns stay empty until then.

How to read it: Compare with the stock's own normal: delivery % 10+ points above its average (highlighted) or rel. delivery 2x+ = unusual holding interest. Price up + rel. volume 2x + rel. delivery 2x = the strongest 'money arriving' sign (filter: 'Money arriving'). High volume with low delivery % = mostly intraday speculation. Price down with high delivery = serious selling.

Turnover (today, 1 week, 1 month, 3 months)

What it is: Turnover = price × volume = how many rupees were traded (approximate). Shown in ₹ crore for today and totals for the last week, month and 3 months.

Why it is in the dashboard: Turnover shows where the biggest money is actually flowing. High-turnover stocks are liquid (easy to buy and sell) and are usually where institutions are active.

When to use it: Daily: sort by today's turnover to see the most active stocks. Compare today with the 1W/1M totals to see if activity is rising.

How to read it: Today's turnover much bigger than usual (1W total ÷ 5) = unusual activity. Filter 'Turnover today ≥ ₹100 Cr' shows the most liquid names.

vs 10 / 20 / 50 / 200 DMA and from 52-week high

What it is: How far the price is above (▲) or below (▼) each moving average, in %. 'From 52W high' = how far below its one-year high the stock is. NEW HIGH / NEW LOW badges mark stocks at 52-week extremes today.

Why it is in the dashboard: Shows each stock's own trend. Stocks above all their averages and near highs are the market leaders.

When to use it: When choosing between stocks: prefer the ones in strong trends, especially in Easy Money.

How to read it: ▲ above all four averages = strong uptrend. Close to the 52W high (within 5%) = leader. Very far above the 10/20 DMA = stretched, may pause. Below the 200 DMA = long-term downtrend.

Sector rotation heatmaps (10 & 20 DMA daily, 50 DMA weekly)

What it is: Each row is a sector, each column a day or week; the color shows % of the sector's stocks above that moving average. Green = most stocks in uptrend, red = most in downtrend.

Why it is in the dashboard: Shows how money moves between sectors over time - something a single table can't show.

When to use it: Weekly review, and whenever you want to know which sectors are turning.

How to read it: 10 DMA daily = earliest signal, 20 DMA daily = confirmation, 50 DMA weekly = bigger trend. A row turning from red to green in all three = money really flowing in. Daily rows turning red while the weekly is still green = sector may be starting to weaken.

Index returns and equal-weight (EW) indices

What it is: Returns of each index over 1 day to 1 year. (EW) lines are calculated by this tool from the group's stocks, giving every stock the same weight.

Why it is in the dashboard: Normal indices are weighted by company size, so a few giants dominate. EW shows how the average stock did - the real experience of most investors.

When to use it: Weekly, to compare large, mid, small and micro caps.

How to read it: EW doing better than the normal index = broad market strong. Normal index up but EW down = a few big stocks are carrying the index.

Index comparison chart (% change)

What it is: All indices and EW lines start at 0% one year ago, so you can see who is leading and who is lagging.

Why it is in the dashboard: Quickly shows whether mid and small caps are confirming Nifty's moves.

When to use it: Weekly, and when Nifty makes new highs or breaks down.

How to read it: Small/mid rising faster than Nifty = broad rally. Nifty rising while small/mid fall = narrow rally, a warning. Click legend names to hide or show lines.

% above moving averages chart (with regime background)

What it is: The history of % of stocks above 10/20/50/200 DMA under the Nifty chart. Background green = Easy Money days, red = Hard Money days.

Why it is in the dashboard: Lets you see breadth trends and divergences over time, not just today's number.

When to use it: Weekly review, and when Nifty is near important highs or lows.

How to read it: Nifty making a higher high while the breadth lines make a lower high = divergence (warning). Breadth rising from below 20% while Nifty is still falling = early sign of a bottom.

A/D line chart

What it is: A running total of (advances - declines) every day. Its direction matters, not the number.

Why it is in the dashboard: It shows the long-term trend of participation. Divergence between Nifty and the A/D line is one of the oldest warning signs in markets.

When to use it: Weekly review, especially near index highs.

How to read it: Nifty up + A/D line up = healthy. Nifty up + A/D line down = warning. Nifty down + A/D line up = broad market stronger underneath.

52-week highs vs lows chart

What it is: Daily bars: green = new 52-week highs, red = new 52-week lows.

Why it is in the dashboard: Shows whether leadership is expanding or damage is spreading over time.

When to use it: Weekly review.

How to read it: Green bars growing = strong market. Red bars growing while Nifty is near highs = hidden weakness.

Compare groups charts (% above 20 / 50 / 200 DMA)

What it is: The breadth history of each group on one chart.

Why it is in the dashboard: Shows which size group turns first. Small and micro caps usually lead - both at tops and at bottoms.

When to use it: Weekly review, and at possible turning points.

How to read it: Small/micro breadth falling while Nifty 500 holds = early warning. Small/micro turning up first after a fall = early recovery sign.

Index charts (separate panes)

What it is: Daily candle charts of each index stacked with the same dates, like a TradingView multi-pane layout.

Why it is in the dashboard: Lets you compare the shape of each index side by side - highs, lows and breakdowns.

When to use it: Whenever you want to check whether one index is making a new high or low while others are not.

How to read it: Hover to see values. Scroll to zoom, double-click to reset.

Educational tool only - not investment advice. Free Yahoo Finance data can be delayed or contain errors. Turnover is approximate (close × volume).
